prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which a magic-wavelength lattice made it possible to bring atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part on optical lattice clocks, credited to Katori and Ye. What the exchange added is a sharper reason. Five members arrive at the same two names from different starting points, but I do not count that as evidence. The evidence is that the 10^-18 performance has been reproduced and compared between independent laboratories (RIKEN and Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL), that the central idea (a lattice at the magic wavelength, with no first-order light shift) is simple enough to state in one line and is checkable, and that the same instruments now give new measured quantities: gravitational redshift over millimetres and tight limits on drifting constants. For a theorist who lives by whether different codes and different groups agree, clock-to-clock agreement at this level is as strong as a result gets. The citation should isolate the lattice concept and its realisation, so that it is clearly distinct from the comb (2005) and ion-control (2012) citations, and it should not mention the redefinition of the second, which is a consequence and not the discovery. A single part is the right size: any second part would need names beyond the three-person limit or would weaken a clean attribution.
statement.case_against: The reservations stand and I do not think they have been answered by argument, only by judgement. Ye already shares the 2005 prize, and a third prize in precision time and frequency can be read as a continuation of a line the committee has honoured twice. The SI second has not yet been redefined. The Sr-lattice priority history is something none of us has verified from the record, and the committee should not fix names before the expert reports on Katori, Ye and the contributions of the SYRTE, NIST, PTB groups and of Hall, Peik and Hollberg are in hand. If those reports show that the lattice concept or the first demonstrations belong materially to someone outside the pair, I would revisit the configuration and would then look first at B013 with a defensible triple, not at a larger clock prize.

responses.point: He prefers B013 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a mature, general mechanism confirmed for fifteen years, and argues that the time-reversal-symmetric Z2 class is distinct from the 2016 topological-phases prize.
responses.response: His case for the Z2 mechanism is the strongest competing one and I take the distinctness argument seriously; as a materials theorist I agree the quantum spin Hall edge channel is not the same discovery as the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz work. What would move me ahead of the clocks is a triple that survives scrutiny. In round 1 I leaned towards Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, and he keeps Mele; the fact that two reasonable members of this committee disagree on the third name, with Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang left out of any triple although they proposed HgTe, is exactly the attribution problem that keeps B013 behind B053 for me this year. If the expert reports show a clear defensible triple restricted to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect, I would put B013 first in a later cycle. I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: She prefers aberration-corrected electron microscopy (B052) as an invention in the statutory sense, and asks whether the committee accepts an instrument prize, noting the uncredited STEM corrector work of Krivanek, Dellby and Lupini and her own proximity as a practising microscopist.
responses.response: I thank her for naming her proximity openly, and I accept the statutory point: invention is a legitimate ground and I use these instruments daily in my own field. But her own reservation about Krivanek, Dellby and Lupini is the one that decides it for me. The TEM and STEM correctors were realised at about the same time, and a citation for Rose, Haider and Urban alone would be contested in the community that actually uses the microscopes. On the instrument question I draw a line that also applies to the clocks: a clock produces a new quantity measured to eighteen digits that tests physics (redshift, constants), whereas the microscope is an enabling tool whose results are credited to the physics it reveals. I would not call that decisive, but together with the unsettled STEM priority it keeps B052 below B053 for me.

responses.point: She supports B053 as precision atomic physics that opens new fundamental tests, but flags the 2005 and 2012 overlap and says contributors such as Lemonde and Ludlow are outside the credited pair; she names B016 as the more natural AMO alternative if the committee prefers a many-body phenomenon.
responses.response: I take her overlap reservation as the main point still open, and her knowledge of the priority history is what I lean on. My answer to the chair's question about whether the 2005 and 2012 prizes are decisive is no: the 2005 citation was for the comb and for laser-based precision spectroscopy, and the 2012 citation for single-ion control, and neither contains a lattice with many atoms and a cancelled light shift. I would, however, ask her directly whether she regards Katori and Ye as sufficient once the expert reports are in, and I accept that Ludlow and Lemonde could not be added without exceeding three names, so the question is whether they are omitted fairly. On B016 I agree it is scientifically attractive, but its five proposed names make a three-person attribution much harder than the clocks.

responses.point: He prefers the experimental Higgs discovery (B046) and lists B053 as an alternative, while asking what has been learned about nature given that the fundamental-physics tests with clocks so far are null results.
responses.response: I defer to him on the physics of the Higgs and I agree that nothing on the list is more securely confirmed. But I do not find his null-result objection decisive for the clocks: limits on drifts of constants and the gravitational redshift test at millimetre scale are positive, quantitative statements about nature at a precision not reached before, and null results of this kind are what a measurement prize rests on. On B046 itself, he states that any trio will look arbitrary and that the shortlist has no agreement on the omitted founder (his list leaves out Jenni, others leave out Della Negra or Virdee). A prize we cannot attribute to a defensible set of three people is not one I can support on this ballot; if the committee can settle that from expert reports I will reconsider, but it is not there today.

uncertainties: Whether the expert reports confirm Katori and Ye as the right and sufficient pair given the Sr-lattice priority history; I rely on atomic-physics colleagues for this and would revisit the names if the reports say otherwise.
How heavily to weigh the 2005 and 2012 precision-metrology prizes, and Ye as a repeat laureate; I regard this as a reservation but not a decisive one.
Whether waiting for the redefinition of the SI second would be wiser; I think the performance is already established, but this is a judgement, not a measurement.

Whether the committee, in this cycle, prefers a new quantum state of matter (B013, B033) to a measurement advance; B033 is young, with an unresolved pairing mechanism, and B013 still lacks an agreed triple.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict for the preferred configuration: my connections are to Uppsala, Los Alamos, B. Johansson and DFT and magnetism collaborators, none credited here, and I have no tie to Katori or Ye. I chaired the 2025 cycle and disclose this as context for B001, which is not in my configuration. For B013, B029 and B052 I have scientific proximity as a materials and magnetism theorist who uses the results, but no personal tie to any credited person.
